discussion.body: The disconnect is striking: universities have EDI infrastructure built to address discrimination, yet the very group experiencing a surge in hate crimes says those offices went silent when they needed them most.

But the survey also shows Canadian students have low negativity toward Jews personally. The hostility is directed at Israel, not Jewish individuals. EDI offices may be struggling to distinguish political criticism from antisemitism — a genuine policy dilemma, not simple indifference.

Research cited in the piece notes higher education usually increases tolerance. The gap between that expectation and what Jewish faculty are reporting suggests something specific has broken in how these offices handle Israel-related tensions.

sources.title: COSI Telescope Comes Together

discussion.body: Gamma-ray telescopes are rare because gamma rays don't focus like light — they penetrate. COSI's wide-field Compton imaging design lets it watch large swaths of the sky for the brief flashes of antimatter annihilation and supernova nucleosynthesis.

The partnership list is notable: a university lab leading, with NASA Goddard, a defense contractor (Northrop), and the Italian Space Agency all contributing. That's the modern model — distributed expertise across sectors and borders.

before.title: NASA's COSI telescope will hunt gamma rays from antimatter and dying stars
before.body: The Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI) is coming together at UC Berkeley. This wide-field gamma-ray telescope will study the Milky Way's most energetic phenomena: the creation and destruction of matter and antimatter, and the final stages of stellar lives. The detector assembly — seen in a July 8 image being lifted into place — uses flex circuits covered in silver material to carry signals to readout electronics. It's a collaboration spanning UC Berkeley's Space Sciences Lab, UC San Diego, the Naval Research Laboratory, NASA Goddard, Northrop Grumman, Space Dynamics Laboratory, the Italian Space Agency, and other institutions.

sources.title: FAA tees up $875M AI tool to help manage air traffic congestion

discussion.body: An AI advisor for the world's most congested airspace is a high-stakes test. If SMART cuts delays and near-misses in the D.C. corridor, the case for nationwide deployment gets much stronger.

The system only *advises* controllers — it doesn't issue commands. That human-in-the-loop design is deliberate, but it also means the AI's value depends entirely on whether controllers trust and act on its suggestions in real time.

Mann's endorsement carries weight: he spent 17 years at the FAA in multiple roles and now advises on aviation safety and AI governance. His 'right call' verdict reflects institutional caution, not just vendor optimism.

before.title: FAA to debut AI air-traffic advisor over Washington, D.C. as soon as Monday
before.body: The FAA's SMART system — an AI tool that predicts traffic flows and flags potential conflicts using airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, and airspace conditions — could go live for the three major D.C.-area airports on September 21. It's the first step toward a planned nationwide rollout across the 29 million square miles of U.S. airspace. Aviation safety consultant Philip Mann, a 17-year FAA veteran, called the limited-scope launch the 'right call' before scaling nationally.

sources.title: What Came Before the American Suburb?

discussion.body: The pre-suburb town wasn't a utopia — it was built on colonized land — but its physical form (dense, walkable, mixed-use) is exactly what urban planners now try to recreate through zoning reform.

The irony: we spent 70 years engineering the suburb, and now spend billions trying to undo its worst effects. Hempstead's Main Street in 1910 had a furniture store, a pharmacy, a commercial block at a street intersection — all within walking distance.

before.title: What the American landscape looked like before the suburb took over
before.body: Before the post-WWII explosion of suburbs, highways, and malls, places like Hempstead Village, New York, show what small-town life looked like. Founded in the mid-1600s under Dutch control, the land was purchased in 1643 by two Englishmen, John Carman and John Fordham, who negotiated with local Indigenous tribes. Families moved in the following year to establish a community centered on a Main Street with storefronts, pharmacies, and commercial blocks — a walkable, mixed-use pattern that vanished once mass automobile ownership and federal highway funding reshaped the country.

sources.title: What Came Before the American Suburb?

discussion.body: The railroad was more than a way out of town: arriving passengers also helped sustain the shops in town.
That makes the later shift toward malls a change in where people gathered and spent money, as well as a change in how they travelled.

after.title: What the American landscape looked like before the suburb took over
after.body: Hempstead Village offers a view of small-town America before postwar suburban expansion. Under Dutch colonial control, John Carman and John Fordham negotiated a land purchase with local Indigenous tribes in 1643; families arrived the following year. Centuries later, railroad connections helped sustain the village's commercial life by bringing people into its downtown shopping district. After World War II, nearby Levittown and shopping malls such as Roosevelt Field helped shift the area's development and drew shoppers away from historic commercial centers.

before.body: Generative AI inference presents unique challenges: models range from tens to hundreds of gigabytes, latency is measured in tokens per second, and cold starts can span multiple minutes as containers and weights transfer, with GPU capacity constrained and traditional monitoring tools lacking token-level signals, as S5E1 describes.
